facts.claim: The Bridge Street crossing is FRA crossing 753183A on the Union Pacific Roseville Subdivision at milepost 206.05.
facts.notes: Confirmed against own stored copy data/fra/crossing-753183A.json, pulled monthly with change log.

facts.claim: The federal inventory records 2 main tracks, 1 siding, and 1 other track at the Bridge Street crossing.
The federal crossing inventory records 8 day trains and 7 night trains, about 15 through trains every 24 hours including the two Zephyrs, at Bridge Street.
facts.notes: The site consistently uses the federal 15/day figure, not the 15-18 press quote (held; see trains-15-18-press-quote).

facts.claim: The Bridge Street crossing carries 10,679 vehicles a day per the 2016 count in the federal inventory.
The Bridge Street crossing is protected by gates with lights per the federal inventory.
The federal inventory records no whistle ban at Bridge Street, so the train horn rule applies in full.
Bridge Street is the only public road crossing of the through tracks at grade in Truckee, and the only such crossing for about eight miles in either direction.
facts.notes: Confirmed via the nearest-crossing records (Stampede Meadows Road east, Old Donner Summit Road west).

facts.claim: The nearest main-line grade crossing to the east is Stampede Meadows Road, eight miles away near Boca, with 1,193 vehicles a day.
The nearest main-line grade crossing to the west is Old Donner Summit Road, fourteen miles away at Norden, with 30 vehicles a day.
Truckee's three other gated crossings (Donner Pass Road and two on Church Street) reach only yard tracks and show zero through trains in the federal record.

Federal regulation 49 CFR 222.21 requires the horn to begin 15 to 20 seconds before every public grade crossing, in the pattern two longs, a short, and a long, held until the locomotive occupies the crossing, with no engineer discretion to skip it.
facts.notes: Page also states the narrow exception: a train stopped close to a crossing may sound less than the full warning.

facts.claim: Federal regulation 49 CFR 229.129 sets the horn's loudness at no quieter than 96 and no louder than 110 decibels, measured 100 feet ahead of the locomotive.

The FRA accident file for Bridge Street holds four incidents (January 1979, May 1981, February 1985, June 1991), all involving automobiles, none with injuries, property damage $500 to $1,000, all in the Southern Pacific era.
facts.notes: Form 6180.57 reports; file current to May 2026.

facts.claim: No accident at the Bridge Street crossing has been reported to the FRA in the thirty-five years since June 1991.
facts.notes: A verified negative: absence of reports in the federal accident file, current to May 2026.

facts.claim: Stampede Meadows Road has seven accidents on file with the FRA through 2021.
facts.notes: Not in today's verified list; drawn from the same FRA accident file as the Bridge Street record.

facts.claim: The horn at Bridge Street can be silenced only by the Town establishing a quiet zone under the federal train horn rule, by upgrading the crossing until engineering carries the safety burden.

The Town of Truckee's Reimagine Bridge Street project lists designating a quiet zone as an explicit goal, alongside new vehicle and pedestrian gates, a rebuilt crossing surface, and new signals at Bridge/Donner Pass Road and Bridge/River Street.
The Truckee town council authorized grant applications toward the roughly $6.3 million Reimagine Bridge Street project in August 2022.
The Town awarded a design contract for the Bridge Street crossing project in January 2025.
The quiet zone component's own cost and timeline are not yet public.
facts.notes: SPEC.md held claim: quiet zone component cost not yet public; the ledger tracks it. Page states the unknown rather than a number.

facts.claim: The Central Pacific built east from Sacramento into the Sierra between 1863 and 1868, and Truckee grew up around the railroad's yards, ice houses, and mills.
The Summit Tunnel at Donner Pass, hand-drilled through granite from four faces at once, opened November 30, 1867.
Track reached the Truckee River canyon and the settlement that became Truckee in 1868.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed the specific date April 3, 1868; the page states the year only.

facts.claim: The golden spike joined the Central Pacific and Union Pacific at Promontory on May 10, 1869, making Donner Pass the mountain gateway of the first transcontinental railroad.
Wooden snowsheds built from the 1860s-70s eventually roofed tens of miles of mountain track and made year-round operation over the pass possible.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed roughly 40 miles of sheds at peak; the page says tens of miles.

facts.claim: In the early Southern Pacific era, surveys for a long summit tunnel and for electrification were studied and shelved.
facts.notes: Verification placed the surveys in 1901-02.

facts.claim: From 1910 the cab-forward steam locomotives, built backward so crews would not suffocate in the snowsheds, took over the mountain.
A second track over the summit opened in 1925, carried through the two-mile Tunnel 41 under Mount Judah, making the mountain a double-track railroad.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed Tunnel 41 length as 10,322 feet, consistent with the page's two-mile description.

facts.claim: The last cab-forward crossed Donner in 1957 and the final steam excursion ran in October 1958; diesels have run the pass since.
The sole surviving cab-forward locomotive stands in the California State Railroad Museum.
Amtrak's train over Donner, until then the San Francisco Zephyr, was renamed the California Zephyr in 1983 when its mid-route alignment shifted to Colorado.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed the renaming took effect July 1983; the page states the year only.

facts.claim: The Donner crossing has hosted passenger trains continuously since 1868.

In 1993 the railroad singled the summit, taking the original 1868 track over the top of the pass, including the hand-cut Summit Tunnel, out of service and moving all traffic to the 1925 alignment through Tunnel 41.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed 6.7 miles of the 1868 alignment were taken out of service.

facts.claim: The abandoned 1868 summit tunnels have become one of the Sierra's most visited hikes.
Union Pacific absorbed the Southern Pacific in 1996, and the line has since been dispatched as UP's Roseville Subdivision.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed the merger closed September 1996; subdivision name confirmed in the FRA inventory.

facts.claim: In 2009 Union Pacific notched the crowns of fifteen tunnels between Rocklin and Truckee, more than 18,000 feet of cutting, clearing double-stacked containers over Donner for the first time.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed the first double-stack train crossed November 19, 2009.

facts.claim: By early 1867 about ninety percent of the Central Pacific's construction force, roughly eleven thousand men, was Chinese, most recruited from Guangdong province.
facts.notes: Verification placed the ninety-percent share by February 1867.

facts.claim: Chinese workers were hired at $26 a month against about $35 for white workers; by 1867 their pay had risen to $35, still below white wages, and unlike white workers they paid for their own food and board.

In June 1867 as many as three thousand Chinese workers struck in the high Sierra for equal wages and shorter tunnel shifts; the railroad cut off their food supply and the strike ended after eight days without concessions.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed the strike began June 24, 1867.

facts.claim: Nitroglycerin was briefly and lethally in use during the Summit Tunnel work.
The winter of 1866-67 brought forty-four storms, and crews lived and worked under the snow in tunnels dug between camp and portal.
Avalanches carried workers away during the 1866-67 winter, some found only when the snow melted.
No one recorded the Chinese construction dead carefully; published estimates of deaths on the Central Pacific run from around fifty to more than a thousand.
facts.notes: Contested by design: the range (~50 to 1,000+) and the fact that nobody counted are the historical record. SPEC.md requires publishing as a range, never a number.

facts.claim: Summit Camp, the Chinese workers' camp beside the Summit Tunnel, was designated a National Historic Landmark in December 2024.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed the designation date December 16, 2024.

facts.claim: In the 1870 census, 407 of Truckee's 1,467 residents were Chinese, making its Chinatown one of the largest in the Sierra.

In 1876 white vigilantes raided Chinese woodcutters' cabins at Trout Creek, burned them, and shot the fleeing men, killing one; the one man tried for murder was acquitted in nine minutes and the arson charges were dismissed.
facts.notes: See trout-creek-date-discrepancy for a held single-date discrepancy within the 1876 record.

facts.claim: One single-date discrepancy exists between sources in the 1876 Trout Creek record.
facts.notes: SPEC.md held claim: verify the specific date before publishing it; the page states the year only and notes the uncertainty in its footer.

facts.claim: In 1878 Truckee's Chinatown was burned and its residents were pushed across the river.
In 1886 town leaders led by newspaperman Charles McGlashan organized a total economic boycott, firing Chinese workers and starving Chinese businesses of custom until the community left Truckee.
facts.notes: Duration of the expulsion is contested; see expulsion-duration.

facts.claim: The 1886 expulsion emptied Truckee's Chinese community within five weeks by one account and ten weeks by another.
facts.notes: Contested: sources disagree (five weeks versus ten); the page states both accounts rather than choosing.

facts.claim: Promoters named the 1886 boycott the "Truckee Method" and campaigned it across California as the respectable way to expel a town's Chinese population.
facts.notes: McGlashan himself campaigned the method statewide.

facts.claim: Nevada County designated the site of Truckee's Chinatown a historical landmark in 2023, and a memorial plaque was placed downtown in 2024.
facts.notes: Verification confirmed the landmark designation June 13, 2023 and the plaque placement May 10, 2024; the page states years only.

facts.claim: Truckee's expulsion was one of scores across the West, alongside the 1885 Rock Springs massacre and the Tacoma and Seattle expulsions, in the shadow of the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act.
facts.notes: Rock Springs and Tacoma dated 1885; Exclusion Act 1882.

facts.claim: Union Pacific fights the Donner winter from Roseville with flanger trains, spreaders, and two rotary snowplows, ex-Southern Pacific machines.
facts.notes: Verification identified the rotaries as SPMW 207 and 222, ex-Southern Pacific, based at Roseville.

facts.claim: Enthusiast accounts describe round-the-clock snow-fighting shifts staged from Truckee when major storms arrive.
facts.notes: Attributed on the page to enthusiast accounts rather than railroad records.

facts.claim: Union Pacific publishes no staffing figures for its mountain snow-fighting operation.
facts.notes: Negative claim; not in today's verified-negatives list.

facts.claim: About 6,500 trucks a day cross the mountain on I-80 at Truckee, per the Caltrans 2024 census at the SR-89 South junction, eastbound leg.
facts.notes: Sourced via the sibling truckee-i80 site, which carries the Caltrans citations.

facts.claim: About 37,000 vehicles a day use I-80 at Truckee per the same Caltrans 2024 census row, with nearby segments running 29,500 to 36,000.
Union Pacific releases no tonnage figures for the Donner Pass line, and the corridor's freight modal share is not published anywhere.
facts.notes: Negative claim; not in today's verified-negatives list.

facts.claim: Roughly forty people a day, on average, board or leave the Zephyr in Truckee in a normal year.
facts.notes: Arithmetic on the verified ridership series (e.g. FY2024: 14,755 / 365 ≈ 40).

facts.claim: The California State Rail Plan's vision reaches Reno from the Sacramento Valley by connecting bus, not by train.
In December 2023 the Capitol Corridor, with a Reno/Sparks extension in its scope, entered the federal Corridor Identification planning program, though no service over Donner is designed or funded.
No public agency has published a study of diverting I-80 truck freight to rail over Donner.
facts.notes: Verified negative: absence confirmed in today's pass across the corridor planning record.

facts.claim: No modern proposal exists to electrify the Donner Pass line.
facts.notes: Verified negative; distinct from the shelved 1901-02 Southern Pacific electrification survey (sp-surveys-1901).

facts.claim: Union Pacific publishes no public schedule of any kind for freight over Donner Pass.
facts.notes: Verified negative: the federal crossing inventory's train count is the only citable freight frequency figure.

facts.claim: Amtrak publishes no official public interface for live train data; this site relies on the community Amtraker mirror of Amtrak's live map.
facts.notes: Verified negative.

facts.claim: Amtrak's California Zephyr stops in Truckee twice a day, train 5 westbound in late morning (scheduled 10:33 Pacific) and train 6 eastbound in early afternoon (scheduled 14:01 Pacific).
facts.notes: Confirmed against this site's own half-hourly observation log.

facts.claim: As rendered 2026-08-10, both fully logged stops since the record began departed Truckee within 15 minutes of schedule, with a median delay of 5 minutes.
facts.notes: Snapshot of a page that re-renders through the day; the raw observation log in the repository is the durable record.

facts.claim: The Donner Summit Historical Society's Heirloom newsletter archive spans eighteen years of monthly local history, free with an article index.
Historic Southern Pacific Sacramento Division employee timetables from 1893 to 1980 are available online.
The Donner Pass railroad radio feed is free to listen to, but its terms restrict rebroadcast, so the site links rather than embeds it.
The Truckee Donner Railroad Society operates a live train cam from a caboose beside the line, with railroad radio audio, and maintains a museum and rotary snowplow display.
facts.notes: Link verified working in today's pass.

facts.claim: A 2009 press account quoted 15 to 18 trains a day over Donner Pass.
facts.notes: SPEC.md held claim: not published anywhere on the site; the federal 15/day figure is the citable one and is what every page uses.

facts.claim: A figure of roughly $25-30 million circulates for the cost of Union Pacific's 2009 double-stack clearance project.
facts.notes: SPEC.md held claim: the figure is not in the primary source (UP's own release), so it is held and does not appear on any page.
